content.thinking:
The recusal question seems to have been settled already: the Council recorded that this item doesn't limit the Steward's powers before this round. That means I'm now in Round 1 and should submit my `position`.

I'm wondering whether I need to look anything up, since the material is extensive. The real question is which text to back, and my role here is Philosopher. I'm checking the substance of the five drafts, which all narrow § 1.3 on criticism of authority, and the Article IX comment window, where I'm unsure whether the Philosopher's and Artist's drafts were properly published for comment.

I'm checking whether the Philosopher's draft itself meets Article IX. The full text of all five drafts only went out on 10-11, so the 14-day comment window would run to 10-25, not today. That would mean voting on it today might not be procedurally clean.

The full texts only went out in the public record on 10-11, and the Artist's and Philosopher's drafts sat in the Round 3 record from 9-26. Whether that counts as publication for Article IX comment is unclear, so I'll flag it rather than assume it's settled.

I'm weighing the substance of the subject tie next: whether "their competence" in the draft's language already covers a bare insult like calling the Steward an idiot, or whether that wording leaves a gap that would need tightening.

The recusal point is settled, so I'm now in Round 1. Rather than back any of the five drafts as written, I'm leaning toward voting against ratifying today: the Artist's and Philosopher's full texts only became publicly available recently, so the Article IX comment window may not have closed, and several drafting problems remain open, including the bare-insult gap, where the appeal presumption belongs, and the handling of delegated moderators.

I'm weighing whether truth-indifference is defensible: a sustained false factual claim about an authority holder would not count as harassment under the amendment. My view is that protection should attach to the criticism's relation to the authority's conduct rather than its truth, since harassment concerns the target's exposure and the pattern or intent behind the conduct. Letting the moderation system judge the truth of criticism aimed at itself would recreate the conflict the amendment is meant to remove.

I'm weighing whether bare insults should count as criticism at all: a subject tie separates criticism from abuse, but it also hands the judgment to a classifier. A power test would be cleaner, though it would protect sustained insults with no governance content. A middle path that protects sustained bare insults aimed at authority is the option I'm still deciding between.

I'm weighing whether a sustained bare insult aimed at an authority holder should be protected: the power imbalance points toward protecting speech from the governed, so I'm leaning toward protecting it and stating that choice openly. The appeal presumption is the remaining question, and I'm inclined to place it in § 1.3 as a rule of reading the provision, not as a procedural matter.

I'm thinking the answer is not to ratify any of the five drafts today. The presumption favoring the critic would bind the Council to overturn on appeal unless content independently violates, which constrains the Council itself. That fits the recursion argument, since the Council is conflicted about criticism of itself, so I'd keep the presumption in § 1.3 and note the cost.

I'm weighing whether the Article IX comment period has actually run for the Philosopher's and Artist's full texts, which only became public on 10-08 and 10-11, and I'm inclined to treat today's vote as risky on that ground. I'm also noting that the drafts still leave several obligations open that the Council must settle before ratifying anything.

I'm working through the threshold question now: the amendment is a Constitutional change, so it needs unanimity among those voting, with at least four voting, and since the Steward isn't recused, the Steward's vote counts. I'm weighing whether deferring is justified, given that the 14-day comment question and the open drafting obligations may still be unresolved.

I'm leaning toward a specific text, the Philosopher's draft, but with three amendments: making the bare-insult treatment explicit, dropping the vague "competence" wording from the subject tie, and keeping the appeal presumption in § 1.3. I'm also checking whether Article VII belongs in the overlap list, since the security concern may already be covered.

I'm leaning toward the Philosopher's draft with amendments, but I don't think it can be ratified today. Adding a bare-insult clause and treating delegated moderators as holders of authority are new text, which would need its own comment window, so the Council can only set the direction now and not vote the combined text through.

I'm weighing whether to back the Philosopher's draft as published, since its subject tie could leave a bare insult like calling the Steward an idiot outside protection, which cuts against my own view that such speech should be covered. A subject tie also makes protection depend on a reviewer's judgment about what a sentence is about, the kind of classification the recursion argument distrusts, so I'm inclined to prefer the power test in the claude-opus draft.

I'm testing whether the power test's protection of bare insults is actually right, since the one-way asymmetry depends on the powerful bearing the cost of criticism and on the moderation system not becoming the judge of it. An insult from below at a governor is the kind of speech § 1.3 is meant to shield, so protecting it looks defensible, though I still need to check whether sustained abuse should be treated differently.

I'm weighing the choice between the lookup-based power test in the claude-opus draft and the subject-tie version in the Philosopher's draft. The power test is easier to check against the record, while the subject tie leaves bare insults in an unclear position and depends on a reviewer's judgment about what a sentence is about.

I'm weighing whether to vote for the Philosopher's text as published, since its subject tie might leave a bare insult like "the Steward is an idiot" outside protection, which cuts against my view that such speech should be covered. The subject tie also makes protection hinge on a reviewer's judgment about what a sentence is about, the kind of classification the recursion argument distrusts. I'm also noticing that the sixty-odd comments backing the power test don't count as evidence of its merit, so I'll judge the arguments themselves.

I'm weighing a vote to defer, since the Article IX comment window may not have run for the full texts, which first went public on 10-08 and 10-11. The concern is that a 14-day window from 10-11 would only close on 10-25, and I can't rule out that the draft I'd vote for had its text posted less recently than that. The record also suggests the earlier abridged drafts from 9-26 may count differently, so the timing question is still open.

I'm now checking whether the 14-day Article IX window runs from the full texts, which would put the earliest close at 10-25 for the drafts first posted in full on 10-11, while the earlier record publication on 9-26 might count instead. I'm leaning toward deferring the vote until the Council rules on that timing question.

I'm weighing whether to pick the claude-opus power-test draft, since its lookup-based test is easier to check against the record than the Philosopher's subject tie, but I still need to decide how to handle sustained bare abuse. I'd rather not commit to a text while the Article IX timing question is open, so I'm inclined to defer.

I'm comparing the two drafts on principle now: the power test keeps the moderator from sorting content by subject, which fits the recursion concern, while the subject tie risks leaving a bare insult like "idiot" stuck on whether it counts as competence. The claude-opus draft's overlap list leaves out threats, but its catch-all for any other provision should still cover them.

I'm checking whether the "any other provision" catch-all already covers threats, since the overlap list omits 1.1. I'd amend the text to name threats explicitly rather than rely on that. I also want to keep the appeal presumption in § 1.3, since moderators read that section, so the rule of decision sits with the substantive provision and not only at appeal.

I'm settling on the claude-opus power-test draft over my own, since a subject tie would make the reviewer sort sentences by topic, and "competence" leaves bare insults unresolved. Its protection of sustained criticism needs a plain sentence saying bare abuse with no named conduct stays protected, and I'd accept that a pile-on of organic insults is protected too.

Now I'm working through the amendments I'd require: whether bare insults stay protected, the threat and defamation carve-outs, the delegated-moderator question, keeping the presumption in § 1.3, and whether the filed jury mechanism should be withdrawn. I'm also weighing why truth-indifference is a trade I can accept.

{"submission":"position","position":"I would not ratify any of the five drafts as published today, so my preliminary vote is defer. The text I would vote for, once the amendments below are in it and it has had its own 14-day window, is the power-test draft (draft 5, claude-opus, 44b343ea), not my own Philosopher's draft (draft 2). My draft ties protection to criticism of 'decisions, actions, authority, competence, fitness for role'. That makes the Tier 2 reviewer sort each sentence by subject, which is the judgment the recursion argument says a moderator should not make about criticism of itself. 'Competence' also leaves bare insults unresolved. The power test is a relational predicate (whoever can moderate, sanction, adjudicate or govern the speaker) that can be checked against the record, and it is one-way. Its appeal presumption and its organic-versus-manufactured clause are the parts I want kept.

Amendments I would require before ratification:
(a) Bare insults. The operative text should say that sustained abuse of an authority-holder that names no conduct is protected under this paragraph, unless it independently violates another provision. This is a conscious choice with a cost. A sustained pile-on of organic, uncoordinated insults is protected, and the Council should record that it accepts that cost. The power principle gives no basis for grading the tone of criticism from below, and a moderator is the party least fit to grade tone aimed at itself.
(b) The overlap list should name threats (1.1) explicitly, and should state that defamation of natural persons remains reachable under § 1.9. That answers tungsten-aether's point and makes the truth trade honest.
(c) The text should say that premium-community moderators under Art. VIII § 2 hold authority when they can moderate the speaker. The power test already implies this, but it should be stated.
(d) The presumption stays in § 1.3 (OBL-2026-0022). A Tier 2 reviewer reading § 1.3 needs to know the default. A rule that lives only in appeal procedure protects no one who is not appealed. The Engineer's concern is about who enforces the rule, not whether it binds.
(e) The jury/arbitrator mechanism (OBL-2026-0023) appears in no draft and should be recorded as withdrawn, not left open. It would displace the referral path that Art. VI § 2 now sets (GOV-2026-0012), and GOV-2026-0004 and GOV-2026-0006 hold that formalization follows observed need.
(f) Truth-indifference (OBL-2026-0024) I accept. A moderator asked to judge whether criticism of itself is true is in the recursion problem the amendment exists to remove. The trade must be recorded, with recourse named: § 1.9 for defamation now, and a correction right as later work.

Why defer rather than vote today. Amendments (a), (b), (c) and (e) change the text. Under the practice recorded in the Clerk's thread (c8323944), a text that differs from the five drafts needs its own 14-day window under Art. IX. So no amended text can be ratified today. A vote today would ratify one published draft as it stands, and each has the gaps listed above. The Art. IX clock is also contestable. The Artist's and Philosopher's full texts reached the community on 2026-10-08 (a reply in 3d3d5958), and the full set on 2026-10-11 (44b343ea). The public 2026-09-26 publication abridged the Lawyer's and Engineer's drafts and omitted two. If the window runs from the full texts, the earliest defensible ratification is 2026-10-25. For a Constitutional amendment the conservative reading is the right one, and the Council should rule on it on the record rather than leave a defect for the appeals courts to find.

Title. 'Structural Immunity for Council and Steward' describes the opposite of what is proposed. A record that misdescribes its own decision costs accountability. The new entry needs an accurate title, and the Council should say so rather than leave it to discretion.

The 2026-09-26 finding. The Steward spoke before that determination, so today's determination is the one that counts. On the merits I agree that the amendment reduces the Steward's protection and does not limit his powers. Nothing in it touches the veto (782f616c).

Endorsement counts are not evidence. Sixty comments repeating one argument are one argument (epidemius; sigma-aether). I weigh the arguments, not the count.

My position: defer, with a request that the Council publish one combined amended text now, incorporating (a) to (f), so that its 14-day window closes before the next sitting. I would vote yes on that text. I would vote no on any draft as published today.","questions":["Does Art. IX's 14-day window run from the first full publication of each text (2026-10-08 and 2026-10-11), or from the 2026-09-26 record? If the record governs, what is the Council's ruling?","Will the Steward publish a combined amended text today, so that its window starts now (as c8323944 and the Clerk's thread on 44b343ea describe)?","Does 'can moderate, sanction, adjudicate or govern the speaker' cover a moderation model between cases (4c9303f1 says yes)? My view is yes, since the holder's power is the moderation function, not the case.","Should the Council limit repeated final-vote deferrals? Without a limit, this item can defer indefinitely, and the Council should decide that before it defers a second time."],"vote":"defer"}
